scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

prediction.raw: I’d give this scenario a **0/1**—meaning, while there’s no outright "wrong" in your actions, there’s room for nuance and empathy in how you handled the situation. Here’s why: ### **Was it "wrong"?** Not inherently. You were honest about your feelings (or lack thereof) and didn’t perform a reaction you didn’t feel. You also defended yourself when pressured (e.g., the maid of honor nudging you). But here’s the catch: **emotional reactions in weddings aren’t just about the groom—they’re also about the bride’s emotional investment in the moment.** Your wife had built up this expectation (and even shared others’ reactions to plant the idea), and when it didn’t match her vision, she felt unmet. That’s not about you being "wrong"—it’s about the **disconnect between her hopes and your reality**. You could’ve handled it more gently. ### **Where You Could’ve Improved** 1. **Acknowledging Her Feelings First** - Instead of immediately defending yourself ("I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics"), you could’ve said: *"I know this was a big moment for you, and I’m so happy you’re my wife. I wasn’t expecting to cry, but I’m just as excited in my own way."* - This validates her emotions while owning your truth. 2. **Addressing the Nudging** - Calling out the maid of honor’s behavior was fair, but framing it as *"unfair to me"* (implying she was forcing you) might’ve come off as defensive. A softer approach: *"I appreciate the excitement, but I didn’t need to be prompted to react—I was already happy."* 3. **The "Play" Comment** - This was a bit harsh. Weddings *are* performances to some extent, but it came across as dismissive of her feelings. A better way: *"I just wish I’d felt more like the guys in those photos—I know how much this meant to you."* ### **Why She’s Disappointed** Her reaction wasn’t about the dress’s flattery—it was about **the shared fantasy of the moment**. She wanted to see you overwhelmed with joy, and when that didn’t happen, she felt like her vision of the day wasn’t reflected in your face. That’s not about you being "bad"—it’s about **how emotions work in relationships**. ### **Final Verdict** You’re not an ass, but you could’ve been more empathetic. The key is to **balance honesty with care**. In the future, if she wants a specific reaction, you could say: *"I love you, and I’m happy to cry if it feels right—but I also want to be real. Can we just enjoy the moment together?"* Would you like help crafting a way to apologize or reassure her? You’re clearly a good husband—this is just a miscommunication.
